items.headline: Report: Nvidia's board is preparing to oust Jensen Huang
items.summary: A Wall Street Journal report that Nvidia's board is preparing to remove Huang sent the stock down about 8% after hours, says @GavinSBaker, who argues the board should finish its independent investigation first, or put any earlier move to a shareholder vote. By early Thursday @KobeissiLetter reported the stock had climbed about 6% off its low, still roughly 5% under Wednesday's close, as traders pared bets on a firing. @naval: "one does not just simply replace the founder."
items.short: A WSJ report says Nvidia's board may remove Huang; the stock fell, then pared losses.

items.headline: Nebius Q3: $981M revenue, and prepayments now cover more than the capex
items.summary: Nebius reported Q3 revenue of about $981 million against roughly $908 million expected, per @KevInvestingYT and @EndicottInvests. @demian_ai's recap of the release: customers committed more than $12 billion since the start of the quarter, prepayments covered over 100% of the capex behind Q3 deals (50-60% three months earlier), GPU-hour prices rose 22% on average from Q2, and Databricks, Datadog and Snowflake signed for the first time. @EndicottInvests reports 2027 capex guidance of $40-45 billion, at least $18.5 billion of it expected from prepayments.
items.short: Nebius beat on revenue and says prepayments now exceed the capex on new deals.

items.headline: Jukan: Nvidia's Rubin slips again, volume shipments now 2027
items.summary: Following a Taiwan rumor that Nvidia had cut orders, @jukan05 says he has confirmed that Rubin has been delayed again, this time by motherboard warpage (the HBM issue was resolved in October), pushing volume shipments to 2027; Nvidia has raised Blackwell orders in the meantime. A source told him a widely shared claim of 30% CCL order cuts was false.
items.short: Rubin volume shipments reportedly slip to 2027; Blackwell orders rise.

items.author: Daniel Koss
items.text:
Who decides Jensen Huang's fate at $NVDA?

X is full of strong opinions. Let's look at the facts.
Then I'll share what I believe is currently happening behind the scenes.

There are 11 directors on the board.
Jensen is the only one who isn't independent.
Removing him takes a simple majority for the decision: 6 votes.

Nvidia has no chair. Lead independent director Stephen Neal (77, a white-collar defense lawyer) runs the process.

The 10 independent directors (number in bracket represents an estimate how much money they made from NVDIA stock).

The founding loyalists:
1) Mark Stevens (since 1993, ~$7.5B): Sequoia partner when it backed Nvidia in 1993. Sold ~$1.4B of stock this year.
2) Tench Coxe (1993, ~$5.9B): Sutter Hill co-led Nvidia's first $2M round.
3) Harvey Jones (1993, ~$1.6B): advised Jensen in the earliest days.
4) Brooke Seawell (1997, ~$0.6B): has chaired the audit committee for decades.

Jensen made them ~$15.6B. They've known Jensen for 30+ years.

The swing votes:
5) Stephen Neal (2019, ~$38M): his old firm Cooley has been Nvidia's outside counsel since 1993, but he's a career white-collar investigator.
6) Dawn Hudson (2013, ~$162M): chairs the committee that sets Jensen's pay.
7) Aarti Shah (2020, ~$12M): her son works at Nvidia.

The independents:
8) John Dabiri (2020, ~$6M): Caltech academic.
9) Melissa Lora (2023, ~$3M): has never sold a share.
10) Suzanne Nora Johnson (July 2026, ~$0): joined from Goldman Sachs.

Ousting Jensen needs all 3 independents AND all 3 swing votes, or at least 1 founding loyalist turning on him.

The board is reportedly "preparing to oust" him. If that's true, someone from the old guard may already have flipped.

My personal view:

The board knows full well it is clearly in Nvidia's economic interest to keep Jensen for as long as they can.

Jensen is Nvidia. He is their vision, their heart, their foundation. And he personally owns many of their most important relationships.

I think they will do everything in their power to keep him in the CEO role, within the laws and rules they are bound by.

Their key task will be to find plausible deniability for keeping him, without violating any rules or laws themselves.

Their incentive to keep him is 100% clear to me. The question is whether they can justify it without putting themselves at risk of neglecting their legal or board duties.

items.title: Joe Hudson's 7 operating rules
items.author: Codie Sanchez
items.summary: From a conversation with Joe Hudson, who coaches leaders at OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Apple: kill 1:1s and bring problems to the whole team, rotate who runs recurring meetings, let anyone stop a bad meeting, and have every employee run five experiments a quarter on their own job. He also says to ask for pushback rather than sell an idea, build the part you understand least first, and end every email with a named owner, action and deadline.

items.title: The money is not in the robot
items.author: Ren
items.summary: A layer-by-layer map of the humanoid supply chain: brains, sensors, edge inference, motors, joints, hands, actuators, power electronics and rare-earth magnets. Ren's argument, backed by a Goldman scorecard, is that the bottleneck and the margin sit in the mechatronics in the middle, especially strain-wave gears and roller screws, rather than in the robot makers or the brain.

items.headline: A waist-based obesity definition beats BMI at predicting death risk
items.summary: In a Nature study of more than 844,000 adults across cohorts in China, Spain, the UK and the US, a framework that adds waist circumference and related measures to BMI, and separates clinical from preclinical obesity by organ dysfunction, outperformed BMI alone at diagnosing obesity and stratifying mortality risk. BMI missed a sizable share of people whose excess body fat carried elevated risk.
items.short: Adding waist measures to BMI better predicts mortality.

items.headline: The blood-brain barrier stops importing protective proteins early in Alzheimer's models
items.summary: Researchers mapped 861 blood proteins and found 92 that cross into the brain, most made in the liver. In Alzheimer's-model mice, the barrier stopped importing protective proteins such as APOA1 before it began to break down; engineering the liver to make more APOA1 reduced disease markers, including astrocyte fat build-up and inflammation.
items.short: Early Alzheimer's may starve the brain of liver-made protective proteins.

items.title: Four Cards
items.rule: If a person is drinking beer, they must be over 21.
items.explanation: Drinking beer could hide something that breaks the rule; Age 16 breaks it if the other side turns out to be Drinking beer. Age 40 can't break it (the rule never says only those cards have it), and Drinking soda isn't covered by the rule at all. Most people pick the card that matches the rule's second half instead of the one that could falsify it. Most people get this version right and the letters-and-numbers version wrong, though the logic is identical.
